Article Title: A West Virginia boy was raised by his aunt after his father killed his mother; a lower court ordered shared custody with paternal grandparents, but the state Supreme Court directed that the aunt recei
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Boy was placed with his aunt after his mother's death

Lower court ordered joint custody with grandparents

Supreme Court questioned the joint custody arrangement

Aunt received sole custody under the final direction

A child who loses his mother at just five months old can face another major disruption if the home and family he has grown up with are suddenly changed. In West Virginia, a custody dispute involving a young boy raised by his maternal aunt reached the state's highest court after his paternal grandparents sought a permanent place in his life. The case raised questions about family relationships, the child's emotional stability and whether grandparents should receive preference over a relative who had cared for him since infancy.In an opinion issued on November 9, 2026, the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia reversed a lower court's joint custody arrangement and directed that the boy's legal and physical custody be placed with his maternal aunt. The ruling, available on Justia, found that dividing custody between the aunt and paternal grandparents would expose the child to unnecessary conflict. The court concluded that remaining with the aunt offered the stability and continuity necessary for his wellbeing.The case began in May 2021, when the child's father fatally stabbed his mother. The father was subsequently convicted of voluntary manslaughter, and his parental rights were terminated. At the time of the incident, the boy was approximately five months old. He was placed with his maternal aunt, identified in court documents as S.M.,who became his primary caregiver. She continued raising him throughout the abuse and neglect proceedings, which extended over several years.The paternal grandparents initially lived in Baltimore, Maryland, but owned a home in Charleston, West Virginia. They began living in their Charleston property around September 2021 as the custody proceedings developed. They sought visitation and placement and later expressed their intention to adopt the child. Their home was subsequently assessed and found suitable for consideration as an adoptive placement. However, the child's aunt and maternal grandmother also sought greater involvement in the proceedings and supported keeping him with the aunt.After several hearings, the Kanawha County Circuit Court considered evidence about both families, their homes and their relationships with the child. The court found that the aunt had developed a close bond with the boy. He called her 'mom' and considered himself the twin of her biological child, who was around the same age. The aunt also testified that she worked as a nurse practitioner focusing on psychological care and had helped address the child's behavioural difficulties and developmental delays.The paternal grandparents also had a relationship with him, and their home was considered suitable. However, concerns emerged about their continued relationship with their son, the child's father. The grandparents visited him in prison several times a month, spoke with him frequently and shared information about the custody proceedings. The paternal grandmother also acknowledged sending him photographs of the child. The aunt and child welfare officials were concerned that the grandparents might struggle to maintain the court-ordered separation between the boy and his father after his release from prison.Despite these concerns, the circuit court ordered joint legal and physical custody in September 2025. It subsequently established a schedule under which the aunt would serve as legal custodian in odd-numbered years and the paternal grandparents in even-numbered years. Major decisions concerning education, medical care and other matters were to be shared. The arrangement proved difficult to implement, and the parties could not agree on a permanent schedule.The dispute reached the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, which examined whether shared custody served the child's best interests. The justices referred to an earlier case involving a similar family tragedy, where a court had found joint custody between maternal and paternal relatives inappropriate because of the conflict between the families.They concluded that the arrangement in this case was also unworkable. Although maintaining relationships with both sides of the family was beneficial, giving multiple relatives decision-making authority risked placing the child in the middle of their disagreements.The court also examined the grandparents' continued support for their son. They planned to allow him to live in another house they owned after his release, with the paternal grandfather intending to stay with him temporarily. The Supreme Court found it difficult to reconcile this arrangement with their responsibility to protect the child from contact with his father.The court emphasised that the statutory preference for grandparent adoption was not absolute. The child's best interests remained the most important consideration. The justices noted that the aunt had been the child's caretaker throughout the proceedings, which had spanned six years, and had become his mother figure. Removing him from the only home he had known risked further emotional harm after the loss of his mother.The court reversed the September 2025 order and remanded the case with directions to grant the aunt sole legal and physical custody. It also instructed the lower court to provide visitation for the paternal grandparents at a frequency and under conditions it considered appropriate, provided the no-contact order protecting the child from his father was maintained.Overall, the ruling established that a grandparent's statutory preference for adoption does not automatically outweigh a child's established emotional bonds and need for stability. The Supreme Court determined that the aunt's continued care offered the most suitable permanent home, while allowing the paternal grandparents to maintain a relationship through visitation without sharing custody.
Article Summary: The case began in May 2021, when the child's father fatally stabbed his mother. The father was subsequently convicted of voluntary manslaughter, and his parental rights were terminated. He was placed with his maternal aunt, who became his primary caregiver. She continued raising him throughout the abuse and neglect proceedings, which extended over several years. The paternal grandparents initially lived in Baltimore, Maryland, but owned a home in Charleston, West Virginia. They sought visitation and placement and later expressed their intention to adopt the child. The court found that dividing custody between the aunt and paternal grandparents would expose the child to unnecessary conflict.

Article Title: In 2018, EPA began sediment cleanups on Minnesota's St. Louis River; eight years later, the final project addressed 225,000 cubic yards as the wider cleanup crossed 1.9 million cubic yards
Article Text:
(Image credit: Canva)

A river carrying the weight of its industrial past

Eight years of sediment cleanup

(Image credit: Wikimedia Commons)

More than sediment: restoring a living ecosystem

A different relationship with the river

Rivers have always been symbols of movement and sustenance, come what may. But years of industrial activity have polluted the waterway that has supported communities and wildlife.In northeastern Minnesota, the St. Louis River is beginning to tell a different story. A major milestone was reached in May 2026, when the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), alongside the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency (MPCA) and other partners, celebrated the completion of the final sediment cleanup project on the Minnesota side of the river. The latest project addressed 225,000 cubic yards of contaminated sediment at Thomson Reservoir, bringing the total amount of contaminated sediment addressed across the wider St. Louis River restoration effort to more than 1.9 million cubic yards.According to the EPA, in an announcement dated May 26, 2026, the project marked the completion of all eight sediment cleanup projects on the Minnesota side of the St. Louis River Area of Concern, an effort that began in 2018.The St. Louis River is the largest tributary flowing into Lake Superior and forms an important estuary near Duluth, Minnesota. While it is now recognised for its ecological importance, the river has spent much of its history dealing with the consequences of industrial development.Commercial shipping, pulp and paper manufacturing, along with other industrial activities, have left behind pollutants that have, over time, settled on the riverbed.Some of these contaminants included mercury, dioxins, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). These substances are particularly concerning because contamination does not simply disappear once industrial activity stops. The scale of the damage was significant enough for the St. Louis River to be designated an Area of Concern in 1987 under the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. These areas are identified because of substantial environmental degradation and the resulting loss of important ecological and human uses of the waterway.According to MPR News, people who grew up around the Cloquet area even recalled a time when the river was referred to as 'Stinktown'. Swimming, fishing and eating fish caught from its waters were activities that residents were discouraged from undertaking.The first of the eight sediment cleanup projects on the Minnesota side began in 2018, when the EPA and its partners removed approximately 37,000 cubic yards of contaminated sediment from Minnesota Slip in Duluth. Over the following years, work continued across several locations, including commercial shipping slips in the Duluth-Superior harbour and other stretches affected by historical industrial pollution. The methods used to address the contamination varied depending on the conditions at each site. In some places, crews dredged contaminated sediment from the riverbed, while other locations required remedial caps to prevent pollutants from entering the aquatic food chain.The final project was undertaken at Thomson Reservoir in Carlton, approximately 15 miles upstream of Duluth. The $30.5 million project addressed 225,000 cubic yards of contaminated sediment and took two years to complete. MPR News stated that approximately 20,000 tons of activated carbon were spread over the water. As the material settles to the bottom, it binds to contaminants, reducing their availability to the organisms that make up the aquatic food web. The contamination is still present in the sediment, but the treatment is intended to prevent it from remaining biologically available and posing the same threat to the ecosystem.The EPA reported that restoration partners have completed 17 habitat projects across the wider Area of Concern, restoring more than 1,000 acres of habitat. More than 80,000 pounds of manoomin, also known as wild rice, have been seeded as part of these efforts.One example of the wider restoration work was a project along the Duluth shoreline, completed in 2021, which involved removing nearly 20,000 dump trucks' worth of old timber waste that had accumulated in the river. The discarded material had been suffocating aquatic life at the base of the food chain. The financial investment behind the restoration has also been substantial. According to the EPA, the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative provided $250 million towards the wider effort, including $187 million under the Great Lakes Legacy Act. These funds helped secure another $208 million in contributions from state, local and industrial partners.Perhaps one of the most encouraging signs of progress is the changing relationship between local communities and the St. Louis River. Places that were once associated with industrial pollution are increasingly becoming spaces where people can spend time outdoors. MPR News reported that more people are now fishing, paddling and even swimming in stretches of the river, activities that would have been difficult to imagine during the years when residents were warned against contact with its waters.However, the May 2026 announcement does not mean that the entire restoration effort is now complete, as it concerns the completion of the eight sediment cleanup projects on the Minnesota side. Further work remains on the Wisconsin side, while a separate wetland restoration project at Mud Lake in Minnesota is also expected to be completed in 2027. There is also the wider question of removing the St. Louis River from the Great Lakes Area of Concern list. Of the nine environmental impairments originally identified, four have been removed so far. The remaining designations will depend on continued restoration and monitoring to demonstrate that the river has recovered sufficiently.
Article Summary: The St. Louis River is the largest tributary flowing into Lake Superior. It forms an important estuary near Duluth, Minnesota. The river has spent much of its history dealing with the consequences of industrial development. In May 2026, the EPA celebrated the completion of the final sediment cleanup project on the Minnesota side of the river. The project addressed 225,000 cubic yards of contaminated sediment.

Article Title: A year after Canada culled more than 300 ostriches on a British Columbia farm over bird flu, the owners are suing, claiming 37 birds are unaccounted for and 1,200 eggs were seized and never returned o
Article Text:
(Image credit: Canva)

Ostriches are flightless birds, but a question that has now resurfaced is: where did they fly off to? As reported by CBC News, in British Columbia, Canada, a dispute that began with an outbreak of bird flu on an ostrich farm has now found its way into another courtroom, almost a year after hundreds of the birds were killed under a government order. The owners of the farm are now suing Canadian authorities, alleging that 37 ostriches have gone unaccounted for and that approximately 1,200 eggs seized during the operation were never returned or compensated for.The eggs, according to the owners, were also central to a planned scientific and commercial venture involving the development of dietary supplements, a business they say could have generated millions in revenue. The new lawsuit has consequently reopened questions about what happened at the farm, the handling of the birds and the consequences of the decision to cull them. The farm, Universal Ostrich Farms, is located in Edgewood, British Columbia, and is owned by Karen Espersen and Dave Bilinski. The dispute dates back to December 2024, when an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), commonly known as bird flu, was detected among the ostriches.The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) became involved after reports of illness and deaths were reported among the flock. According to the agency, two ostrich carcasses tested positive for the H5N1 strain of avian influenza on December 31, 2024, following which it issued an order requiring the farm to dispose of the remaining birds by February 1, 2025. The outbreak had already taken a considerable toll on the flock, with around 70 ostriches dying during the period of infection. However, the owners disagreed with the decision to destroy the surviving birds, arguing that many had recovered and that the remaining flock was healthy. The matter then became a prolonged legal dispute, with the farm challenging the CFIA's decision through the Canadian courts. In May 2025, the Federal Court dismissed the farm's applications for judicial review.By November 2025, the legal battle had reached its conclusion, and the CFIA moved forward with the destruction of the remaining ostriches. However, the farm owners have now come forward to allege that the number of birds accounted for during the operation does not match the number they say were present on the property. According to the lawsuit, 351 ostriches were on the farm when authorities executed their warrants, but compensation was offered for only 314 birds. The owners say this leaves 37 ostriches unaccounted for and that the agency has not provided a satisfactory explanation for the discrepancy. The compensation reportedly offered was $3,000 per bird, amounting to $942,000 for the 314 ostriches. However, this offer was rejected by the owners.But there are accounts of the flock's numbers that differ considerably. In an update published in October 2025 , the CFIA said its estimates placed the number of birds on the property between 300 and 330, adding that the farm had not provided the flock records it had requested. The agency said it could not determine whether the difference between its estimates and the owners' earlier figures resulted from an overreported flock size or deaths that had not been reported.The farm says it had invested in developing the product and was close to launching it when the eggs were seized. It has projected that the venture could have generated more than $200 million in revenue and is now seeking damages for the alleged loss of this business opportunity. The owners argue that the seizure and subsequent disposal of the eggs effectively brought the enterprise to an end. The CFIA, however, has stated that it did not receive documentation demonstrating that the farm was conducting the claimed research or preparing to launch such a product. While this influenza primarily affects birds, certain strains can still infect mammals, including humans. The CFIA has maintained that its decision to order the cull was guided by the need to eliminate the infection from the affected premises and reduce the possibility of further transmission.The latest lawsuit was reportedly filed on October 30, 2026, by Universal Ostrich Farms and Landco Ventures, the company that owns the property leased to the farm. The defendants include the Canadian Food Inspection Agency, the federal government and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP). The CFIA has confirmed that it is aware of the lawsuit and will respond in due course, while the RCMP had not provided a comment to CBC at the time of its report. While the allegations are yet to be tested in court, the lawsuit has brought the controversial culling operation back into focus.
Article Summary: A dispute that began with an outbreak of bird flu on an ostrich farm has now found its way into another courtroom, almost a year after hundreds of the birds were killed under a government order. The owners of the farm are now suing Canadian authorities, alleging that 37 ostriches have gone unaccounted for and that approximately 1,200 eggs seized during the operation were never returned or compensated for. The new lawsuit has reopened questions about what happened at the farm, the handling of the Birds and the consequences of the decision to cull them.

Russia targets Ukraine's power infrastructure

Russia struck six large electricity substations across four central regions of Ukraine, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said on Wednesday, as the second day of peace talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States began in Abu Dhabi.Koretskyi said Russian forces had also targeted railway infrastructure in eastern and central Ukraine, in addition to the attacks on energy facilities.In a post on Telegram, the Ukrainian prime minister said six major electricity substations had been hit, but did not immediately provide details of the damage.Meanwhile, the second day of trilateral peace talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States began in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, Kyiv's chief negotiator confirmed to news agency Reuters.Earlier, Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda reported that Russian forces had attacked energy infrastructure in the Ternopil, Kirovohrad, Rivne, Volyn, Odesa and Zhytomyr regions on the evening of November 3 and overnight into November 4.

Article Title: After 47 years of marriage, a Missouri couple split a joint trust worth nearly $895,000; when the husband died, his wife challenged a promise involving his $505,000 IRA, and a court upheld a medical t
Article Text:
Couple divided nearly $895,000 joint trust

Husband died before IRA arrangement was implemented

Court limits access to major medical expenses

A Missouri couple who had been married for 47 years divided their nearly $895,000 joint trust equally in September 2021, after the husband promised that his separate $505,000 retirement account would cover his wife's extraordinary medical expenses if he died first. But when he was killed in a car accident barely two months later, the widow discovered that she was not named as a beneficiary of the account. A subsequent legal battle over the unwritten promise reached the Missouri Court of Appeals, which on November 10, 2026, upheld a court-created medical trust funded with $505,000 from the husband's estate. In its ruling in 'In the Matter of Ray Bergfeld, Deceased' (ED113884), the Missouri Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court's decision to protect Mary Alice Bergfeld's access to money for major and traumatic medical expenses, while rejecting her request for broader access to the retirement funds.Mary Alice and Ray "Buzz" Bergfeld had been married for 47 years and had children from previous marriages. They maintained separate individual retirement accounts (IRAs) and revocable living trusts to ensure their respective estates would eventually pass to their own children. However, they also established a joint trust in 2006 to provide financial security for both spouses during their lifetimes. By September 1, 2021, the trust held $894,638.75 in a Morgan Stanley account.Buzz wanted to divide the money so he could pass his share to his children while he was still alive. He initially proposed that he receive 60% and Mary Alice 40%, but she rejected the arrangement. After several rounds of negotiations, he eventually offered an equal division.As part of the agreement, Buzz told his wife that if he died first, his son Bob would manage his approximately $505,000 IRA and use it to pay for her extraordinary medical expenses. Any money left in the account after her death would go to his children.Mary Alice agreed to the 50:50 division. On or around September 10, 2021, the couple withdrew the assets from the joint account, divided them and terminated the trust.Unknown to Mary Alice, Buzz had begun consulting an attorney in April 2021 about dividing the joint trust. His financial adviser had referred him to the lawyer, and some of Buzz's children attended meetings. The judgment noted that Buzz asked his attorney to send legal bills to his daughter Mona's home rather than the marital residence so that Mary Alice would not know he had hired legal counsel. He also took his wife's individual estate-planning documents from a safety deposit box without her knowledge and gave them to his attorney.His lawyer reportedly suggested preparing a postnuptial agreement to document the arrangement, but Buzz instructed him not to proceed because he believed Mary Alice would not accept its terms.On November 22, 2021, Buzz died in a car accident. When Mary Alice subsequently asked his son Bob about the IRA, she was told she was not listed as its beneficiary. She later filed a lawsuit against her husband's estate, alleging fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation over the promise concerning the retirement account.In May 2025, the trial court ruled that Buzz had negligently misrepresented the arrangement because he failed to exercise reasonable care in making the promise without putting a plan in place to fulfil it. However, it did not find sufficient evidence that he knowingly made a false promise, which was necessary to establish fraud.The court created an equitable trust funded with $505,000 from Buzz's estate. It restricted the money to major and traumatic medical expenses, including hospital treatment, prescription medicines, rehabilitation, medically necessary equipment and long-term care. Mary Alice appealed, arguing that the money should also cover her general support and that the trust should have taken effect from the date of Buzz's death rather than the 2025 judgment.The appellate court rejected both arguments. It noted that Mary Alice's own income and assets were sufficient to meet her living expenses, even after several hospitalisations and her move to assisted living. At the time of trial, she was 91 years old, earned approximately $100,000 annually and had assets exceeding $1.5 million.The court also rejected her claim of fraudulent misrepresentation, noting that testimony from her daughter supported the finding that Buzz had promised to speak to his son about managing the IRA in the future, rather than claiming that he had already done so.The estate also challenged the negligent misrepresentation finding, arguing that the couple's private financial discussions did not constitute a business transaction. However, the appellate court held that the management and division of their joint trust, involving financial advisers and legal professionals, qualified as a transaction in which Buzz had a financial interest.The Missouri Court of Appeals ultimately affirmed the lower court's judgment, preserving the $505,000 medical trust for Mary Alice while ensuring that any remaining funds after her death would pass to Buzz's children.
Article Summary: Mary Alice and Ray Bergfeld had been married for 47 years and had children from previous marriages. They maintained separate individual retirement accounts (IRAs) and revocable living trusts to ensure their respective estates would eventually pass to their own children. They also established a joint trust in 2006 to provide financial security for both spouses during their lifetimes. Buzz told his wife that if he died first, his son Bob would manage his approximately $505,000 IRA and use it to pay for her extraordinary medical expenses. Any money left in the account after her death would go to his children.

Article Title: On Christmas Eve 1971, 17-year-old Juliane Koepcke fell about 3,000 metres, still strapped to her seat, from LANSA Flight 508, which was struck by lightning over Peru; the only survivor of the 92 peop
Article Text:
Waking up in the jungle

Wandering in the rainforest for 10 days

Day 10: Maggots appeared in her wound\

Juliane Koepcke, 71, has never struggled to recount the Christmas of 1971. She was just 17, flying home to see her father in Panguana. The passengers were already frustrated after a seven-hour delay when the aircraft encountered a violent thunderstorm over the Peruvian rainforest. Fear glistened in her eyes as she saw the lightning around the plane. Scared, she held her mother’s hand tightly. Neither of them could speak. The other passengers began to scream and weep.“After about 10 minutes, I saw a very bright light on the outer engine on the left. My mother said very calmly, ‘That is the end, it's all over.’ Those were the last words I ever heard from her,” Koepcke recounted to the BBC, 40 years after the incident.The plane went into a nosedive, and all she could see was pitch black and the people screaming. The engine’s roar drowned out all other noises. Then the noise stopped, and she was out in the sky, in a free fall, still strapped to her seat. Juliane plunged thousands of metres towards the jungle as LANSA Flight 508 broke apart in mid-air. The last thing she could remember was the whispering of the wind. She felt completely alone.Then nothing. She lost consciousness. She woke up the next day, all alone, and all she could think was, “I survived an air crash.” For the next 10 days, she wandered through the rainforest before being rescued on the eleventh day. She was the only one of the 92 people aboard to walk out of the jungle alive.When she woke the next morning, Koepcke called out desperately for her mother, but there was no response. She was completely alone. Recalling the moments before the crash, she remembered that her mother had grown anxious as the plane entered the heavy clouds. The violent turbulence that followed had made her even more nervous.Before she could gather her thoughts, Koepcke became aware of her injuries. She had a broken collarbone and deep cuts on her legs. She had also lost her glasses and one of her sandals, and she was wearing a sleeveless mini-dress. She had a ruptured ligament in her knee. “My injuries weren't serious, so I could still walk.”Born to German parents in 1954, Juliane Koepcke was raised in the Peruvian jungle, ABC reported. Her father, Hans-Wilhelm Koepcke, was a renowned zoologist, and her mother, Maria Koepcke, was a scientist who studied tropical birds. They had a biological research station called Panguana in the rainforest. Having grown up on the station as a 'jungle child', she knew how to survive.“Before the crash, I had spent a year and a half with my parents at their research station, only 30 miles away. I learned a lot about life in the rainforest, and that it wasn't too dangerous. It's not the green hell that the world always thinks,” she told the British broadcaster.She knew she had to survive alone. So she found a creek and stuck to the water. The only food she had was a bag of sweets from the wreckage, and they didn’t last. She knew the things she had to avoid: snakes camouflaged as dry leaves and the changing weather. She also heard planes overhead searching for the wreckage. But unfortunately, they couldn’t see her through the dense canopy.On the fourth day, she heard a king vulture land nearby. She knew they came down only for carrion. Around a bend in the water, she found a bench seat with three passengers jammed headfirst into the mud. It was her first time seeing a corpse. As a 17-year-old, it wasn’t easy for her. Her first thought was that one of them was her mother. “But when I touched the corpse with a stick, I saw that the woman's toenails were painted. My mother never polished her nails. I was immediately relieved but then felt ashamed of that thought,” she told the broadcaster.By the tenth day, she could barely stand. She drifted along a larger river until she saw what looked like a big boat, and she thought she was hallucinating. But it was real. Up a small path, she found a hut with a palm-leaf roof, an outboard motor and a litre of petrol.By then, the wound on her upper right arm was infested with maggots. It was about one centimetre long. That was when her childhood memories came to her aid. “I remembered our dog had the same infection, and my father had put kerosene in it, so I sucked the petrol out and put it into the wound. The pain was intense as the maggots tried to get further into the wound. I pulled out about 30 maggots and was very proud of myself.”She spent the night there. The next morning, she heard men’s voices outside. “It was like hearing the voices of angels,” she recalled. When they saw her, they froze. They took her for a water goddess from local legend. She spoke to them in Spanish, explained what had happened, and they took her back to civilisation.Ninety-two people were on the plane: 86 passengers and six crew members, according to the Aviation Safety Network. Ninety-one died. Up to 14 of those who survived the impact died while waiting for rescue, and Juliane’s mother was among them. Juliane was the only one found alive who was able to walk out of the jungle.The day after the rescue, she was reunited with her father. He could barely speak. Searchers recovered her mother’s body on 12 January. She later learned that her mother had also survived the initial crash but was so badly injured that she died several days later. Now 71, Koepcke is a biologist. She sees the world just as her parents did. And every detail of Christmas Eve 1971 remains vivid.
Article Summary: Juliane Koepcke, 71, was 17 when LANSA Flight 508 crashed over the Peruvian rainforest. She was the only one of the 92 people aboard to walk out of the jungle alive. For the next 10 days, she wandered through the rainforest before being rescued.

Article Title: Bus driver burnt alive as arson attacks, crude bomb blasts rock Bangladesh
Article Text:
Several buses have been set ablaze and more than 50 crude bomb explosions rocked different locations across Dhaka over the past few days, according to a local media report.

Police step up security, arrest 19

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the most important measure to prevent such incidents? Strengthening police security Strict action against those responsible Improved public surveillance Addressing political tensions through dialogue 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: A 60-year-old bus driver was burnt to death after unidentified miscreants set fire to a parked bus in Bangladesh's Faridpur early Monday, as a series of arson attacks and crude bomb explosions were reported in Dhaka and several other districts.The deceased, identified as Md Kalachan Sheikh, was sleeping inside a bus belonging to Kishore-Tanay Paribahan near Goalchamat New Bus Stand when it was set on fire, reported Bangladesh Daily New Age (Bangladesh). Firefighters rescued him and took him to Faridpur Medical College Hospital, where doctors declared him dead.In another incident, a petrol bomb was hurled at a double-decker bus carrying around 35 students of Islamic University in Jhenaidah on Monday night. The bus, named Diganta, was travelling towards the university campus when the attack took place in the Dragon Bagan area of Shailkupa upazila. No casualties were reported.In Dhaka, at least two crude bombs exploded in front of Tokyo Square in the Mohammadpur area around 9:15pm on Monday. Police said they were yet to identify those responsible.Separately, a Basumati Paribahan bus was set on fire in front of the Mirpur-11 Post Office around 9.30pm.No one was injured.In Bogura district, a van carrying jute sacks was set on fire on the Dhaka-Bogura highway in Sherpur upazila on Monday evening. The vehicle was gutted, temporarily disrupting traffic. Firefighters brought the blaze under control.More buses torched in Dhaka, Savar and GazipurThe incidents came amid a wider spate of arson attacks and crude bomb explosions across Bangladesh. According to The Daily Star, six buses were set on fire in Savar, Dhaka and Gazipur on Monday.In Savar, two buses parked along the Dhaka-Aricha highway were torched in the Genda and Baliarpur areas around 1am and 4am, respectively. One was used to transport garment workers, while the other belonged to Itihash Paribahan. The fires damaged the buses' seats and interiors.In Dhaka, a Lovely Paribahan bus was set on fire beneath the Farmgate metro station in the evening. Another bus, belonging to Basumati Paribahan, was torched under the metro rail line in Mirpur-11 around 9:15pm.In Gazipur's Kaliakair upazila, two parked buses were set on fire in the Chandra area along the Dhaka-Tangail highway, The Daily Star reported.Crude bomb explosions were also reported from several parts of Dhaka, including Banasree, Mohakhali, Dhaka University campus and outside the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court.Amid the attacks, the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) set up 160 additional checkpoints at key locations across the capital on Monday and deployed more personnel to prevent further incidents.DMP Deputy Commissioner (Media) Akhter Hossain told The Daily Star that police had arrested at least 19 people in the preceding 24 hours in connection with recent blasts and attacks. He said many of those arrested were linked to the Awami League, whose activities are currently banned, reported The Daily Star.Police in Savar also suspected the involvement of the banned Awami League in the two bus arson incidents there. Investigations were under way to identify those responsible.The attacks come amid heightened political tensions in Bangladesh following the July 2024 uprising that led to the ouster of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina. The Awami League's activities were subsequently banned, and authorities have alleged links of some of its leaders and activists to recent incidents of crude bomb explosions and vehicle arson.
Article Summary: A 60-year-old bus driver was burnt to death after unidentified miscreants set fire to a parked bus in Bangladesh's Faridpur early Monday. A petrol bomb was hurled at a double-decker bus carrying around 35 students of Islamic University in Jhenaidah on Monday night. Six buses were set on fire in Savar, Dhaka and Gazipur on Monday. More than 50 crude bomb explosions were also reported from several parts of Dhaka.

Article Title: Six journalists killed, 33 years of defiance: Russia's last major independent newspaper shuts down
Article Text:
Ivan Zhilin, journalist of Novaya Gazeta, puts poster with sign 'Novaya Gazeta lived here' to cover the outlet's plaque on the office as the newspaper shuts down, citing what it describes as a campaign by authorities

Crackdown on independent media

Russia's last major independent newspaper critical of the Kremlin, Novaya Gazeta, shut down its Moscow office on Monday after three decades, citing sustained pressure from government officials and security agencies.The newspaper, which has faced mounting restrictions since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, said authorities had forced its editorial team to cease operations.In a statement published on October 30, the newspaper said Russian authorities and security services had "forced our editorial team to cease operations.”“Human rights and freedoms have been abolished in this country, and defending them is now treated as a crime,” the newspaper said, "Elections and elected governing bodies have been effectively dismantled, civil society institutions have been wiped out, freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled underfoot.”On Monday, journalists cleared the Moscow office, slowly taking down portraits of six colleagues who were killed for their work. The photographs had hung in the newsroom where reporters and editors once planned their investigations.As staff gathered outside the building, a new sign was placed above the newspaper's former nameplate. It read, “Here lived Novaya Gazeta.”Tatiana Britskaya, the editor of Novaya Gazeta's investigations desk, said she had expected the newspaper to shut down almost every day over the past four-and-a-half years.“It is an incredibly difficult decision, because this is more than a workplace, more than an office -- this is our home, and we're losing it,” she said.Sergei Sokolov, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, expressed hope that it would eventually return.“We will live, and I am sure that this country, caught in such a terrible era, will eventually stir. As soon as those first signs appear, Novaya Gazeta will return, to our readers and to our colleagues.”Founded in 1993, Novaya Gazeta earned a reputation for investigative journalism, particularly its reporting on human rights violations and corruption in Russia. Six of its journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya, who reported on atrocities during the second Chechen War.Politkovskaya was shot dead in her apartment building in 2006, during Vladimir Putin's first term as president.The newspaper faced increasing government pressure as the Kremlin tightened its grip on critics. The crackdown intensified after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, forcing several independent media organisations to close or move their operations abroad.Novaya Gazeta was fined over allegations that it had discredited Russia's armed forces. Authorities also designated it a “foreign agent”, a label that carries strong negative connotations and exposes those named to additional government scrutiny.Its online platforms were blocked, its printing house was seized, its media registration was revoked and its reader donation system was shut down. The latest order to vacate its Moscow office marked another blow to the publication.Longtime editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov, who shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize with Philippine journalist Maria Ressa, also faced intimidation. In 2022, an attacker poured red paint over him on a train, causing severe irritation in his eyes. Muratov stepped down as editor in 2023 after being designated a “foreign agent”.Some of the newspaper's journalists left Russia in 2022 and established a separate publication, Novaya Gazeta Europe. The outlet continues to criticise the Kremlin and its military campaign in Ukraine.
Article Summary: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last major independent newspaper, shut down its Moscow office on Monday after three decades. The newspaper, which has faced mounting restrictions since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, said authorities had forced its editorial team to cease operations.

Article Title: Indian-origin Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal to challenge trans sports rules: Report
Article Text:
As per the report by Fox News, Republicans say the Democrats' response contradicts their support for the 'No Kings' movement. The movement has organised protests against US President Donald Trump, accusing him of exercising authoritarian power and undermining democratic principles.

Why are Republicans accusing Democrats of hypocrisy

What happened in Washington

Can the voter-approved measures be reversed

Democratic leaders in Colorado and Washington are facing accusations of hypocrisy after signalling plans to challenge or change voter-approved restrictions on transgender athletes competing in girls' sports.According to a report by Fox News, Republicans have accused them of ignoring the people's mandate, pointing to their support for the 'No Kings' movement, which argues that political power should rest with the people and not be concentrated in the hands of leaders.The controversy erupted after voters in the two traditionally Democratic states backed measures restricting transgender students from competing in girls' school sports, the report said. However, Colorado Governor-elect Philip Weiser and Democratic Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal have both criticised the results and indicated that they would explore ways to reverse or modify the measures.Weiser suggested that Colorado's Democratic-controlled legislature could revisit the voter-approved measures. Speaking at his first post-election news conference, he said it was within the legislature's role to consider changes."It is 'statutory … and a natural and I believe appropriate role for the legislature to say ‘what are the adjustments that need to be added," he said.He also raised concerns about how the sports restriction could be implemented."I don’t believe it would be acceptable to Colorado to have every student athlete to have to go through full-body examinations or other invasions of privacy," Weiser added, according to the Denver Post.As per the report by Fox News, Republicans say the Democrats' response contradicts their support for the 'No Kings' movement. The movement has organised protests against US President Donald Trump, accusing him of exercising authoritarian power and undermining democratic principles.Weiser has participated in 'No Kings' protests. Republicans argue that his willingness to revisit a decision made directly by voters goes against the movement's central message.The Adams County Republican Party called the governor-elect "King Phil I" and accused him of treating the election result as a suggestion rather than a mandate."But before the ink on the ballots is even dry, Governor-elect Phil Weiser is already signaling that the vote of the people is merely a ‘suggestion’. With Coloradans approving ballot measures to crack down on fentanyl and protect youth sports and children, Weiser walked up to the podium on Wednesday and essentially declared that the will of the majority needs to pass his personal vibe check first," the party said in a statement.The Colorado House Republican caucus also criticised the Democrats, saying: "If the Democrats truly believe there should be ‘No Kings’ in America, it is time they take their own advice."A similar controversy has emerged in Washington state, where voters approved Initiative 638 with approximately 56% support.The measure bars students defined as "biologically male" from competing in girls' K-12 school sports. It also requires students seeking to participate in girls' teams to provide verification of their biological sex from a healthcare provider.Following the result, Jayapal said Democrats would work to reverse the measure."We're going to start planning for how we overturn these bad initiatives and how we go back to loving everyone with gender inclusivity the way we have for decades," she said, according to local media reports.Republicans and other critics pointed to Jayapal's earlier support for the 'No Kings' movement. They highlighted a November 2025 social media post in which she wrote: "We have democracy for a reason. America doesn’t belong to kings it belongs to the people and we're going to keep it that way."One critic responded: "Rep. Jayapal, this you?"Washington Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad has also indicated support for challenging the measure in court. She called it "unconstitutional on its face" and said the party would "support [for] organizations planning to challenge it in court."The two states have different rules governing changes to ballot measures.In Colorado, the Democratic-controlled legislature could consider amendments to the voter-approved measures. Weiser has indicated that he wants lawmakers to examine possible adjustments.In Washington, lawmakers cannot repeal a voter-approved initiative during its first two years. However, they can amend it with a two-thirds majority in both legislative chambers. After two years, lawmakers can amend or repeal it with a simple majority.The controversy has put Democrats in both states in a difficult position. They must decide whether to respect the restrictions approved by voters or pursue changes through legislative and legal routes.
Article Summary: Democratic leaders in Colorado and Washington are facing accusations of hypocrisy after signalling plans to challenge or change voter-approved restrictions. Republicans say the Democrats' response contradicts their support for the 'No Kings' movement. The movement has organised protests against US President Donald Trump, accusing him of exercising authoritarian power.

Article Title: Advantage China? How Nvidia CEO's affair with 'spy' Alice Huang could impact US
Article Text:
The scandal also puts President Donald Trump in a difficult position, given his close relationship with Huang and Nvidia's importance to his economic agenda. (Photo credit: Social Media/Daily Mail)

Why Nvidia is central to America's AI ambitions

Espionage fears and political scrutiny grow

Trump's ties with Huang complicate US response

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission of an extramarital affair has triggered a political and national security storm in Washington, with questions emerging over whether his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of espionage could have exposed sensitive American technology to Beijing. What might have remained a private matter has now become a major concern for US lawmakers, intelligence officials and the world's most valuable artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker.The woman at the centre of the controversy, Alice Huang, is a former executive at Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, which has faced allegations of helping route advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese buyers in violation of US export restrictions. US intelligence officials have reportedly concluded that she spied for China, although Beijing has rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated. The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has opened an investigation into Megaspeed's activities, while Nvidia's board has launched an independent review of its chief executive's interactions with the businesswoman.The controversy comes at a particularly sensitive time for Washington, which has made maintaining its lead over China in AI a major economic and national security priority.With Nvidia supplying the vast majority of high-end chips powering American AI development, any compromise involving the company could have consequences extending well beyond its leadership, potentially affecting US-China relations, technology exports and the broader AI industry.Nvidia has become one of the most important companies in the global technology industry, with its graphics processing units (GPUs) forming the backbone of modern AI systems and data centres. Originally developed primarily for video gaming, these chips have proved particularly effective at the complex calculations required to train and operate advanced AI models.The company is estimated to control more than 80% of the high-end AI chip market, making it difficult for American technology companies to develop advanced AI systems without relying on its products.This dominance has also made Nvidia central to Washington's efforts to restrict China's access to advanced semiconductor technology. The US has imposed export controls on powerful Nvidia chips since 2022, seeking to slow Beijing's progress in developing sophisticated AI systems that could have military and cybersecurity applications.However, Huang has repeatedly argued that Nvidia should be allowed to sell some less advanced chips, including its H200 processors, to Chinese companies. He believes restricting access could push Chinese businesses towards domestic chipmakers, eventually weakening America's influence over the global AI ecosystem.Megaspeed has previously faced allegations of purchasing advanced Nvidia chips and routing them to Chinese customers. Trade records cited in reports indicate that more than $3 billion worth of chips moved from Singapore to China in a single year, alongside substantial shipments from Malaysia.The immediate concern for American intelligence officials is what information China may have obtained through Alice Huang's alleged connections with Nvidia's chief executive.According to Politico, officials fear Beijing could have gained access to privileged information about Nvidia's chip technology, manufacturing capabilities and future business plans. Such information could help Chinese companies narrow the technological gap with American competitors.Retired General Leslie Beavers, a former Pentagon intelligence official, told Politico that Washington should be particularly concerned about China gaining insights into how advanced chips are manufactured and how their performance and reliability are achieved.Glenn Gerstell, former general counsel for the National Security Agency, warned that the alleged incident highlighted how China's intelligence network could reach into Silicon Valley. He said the private sector was "every bit as important to our national security as the government is".The controversy has also prompted calls for congressional scrutiny. Republican leaders of the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China committees have sought a closed-door briefing with Huang, while Democratic lawmakers have demanded answers about Nvidia's safeguards against foreign espionage.Ro Khanna, ranking member of the House China Committee, called for a classified briefing, saying lawmakers needed to understand the national security risks before deciding on further action.The scandal also puts President Donald Trump in a difficult position, given his close relationship with Huang and Nvidia's importance to his economic agenda.Trump has repeatedly praised the Nvidia chief, viewing the company as central to his ambition of making the US the global leader in AI. The two have maintained regular contact since their first dinner at Mar-a-Lago in early 2025. Huang also accompanied Trump on Air Force One during a state visit to Beijing earlier this year.Trump defended the executive after the controversy emerged, saying he had spoken to him and believed he had no knowledge that Alice Huang was allegedly a spy. "I think he’ll be in good shape," the president said.However, any action against Nvidia could carry significant economic consequences. The company's growth has been closely tied to the AI investment boom, which has also driven gains across the US stock market. Nvidia is a key supplier and investor within an interconnected technology ecosystem involving AI developers, chipmakers and data centre operators.According to Politico, US officials face a difficult choice: failing to address a potential espionage breach could compromise national security, but imposing restrictions on Nvidia could weaken America's own AI industry and potentially benefit Chinese competitors.
Article Summary: N Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission of an extramarital affair has triggered a political and national security storm in Washington. Questions have emerged over whether his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of espionage could have exposed sensitive American technology to Beijing. The scandal also puts President Donald Trump in a difficult position, given his close relationship with Huang and Nvidia's importance to his economic agenda.

Article Title: A New Mexico woman posed as an IRS agent and convinced a victim to pay more than $150,000 in supposed fees to release a promised tax windfall; she has now pleaded guilty to five federal charges
Article Text:
Five federal charges, faces up to 20 years in prison

IRS warns against impersonation and fake refund schemes

How taxpayers can identify suspicious IRS communications

A New Mexico woman impersonated an Internal Revenue Service (IRS) agent and convinced a victim that he would receive a large sum of money from the US tax agency if he first paid various fees and deposits. The victim handed over at least $150,000, believing the money would be transferred to the IRS, but the woman allegedly spent it on personal expenses. According to a November 9 announcement by the US Department of Justice (DOJ), Sandra Vega, 48, of Pecos, has now pleaded guilty to five federal charges in connection with the fraud scheme, which operated for nearly eight years.In her plea agreement, Vega admitted that she posed as an Internal Revenue agent between 2018 and March 2026 to defraud a man identified in court documents as John Doe. She persuaded him that he was entitled to receive a substantial payout from the IRS but needed to pay several fees and deposits before the money could be released.The victim made payments totalling at least $150,000, expecting that Vega would forward the amount to the federal tax agency. However, prosecutors said none of the money was ever sent to the IRS. Instead, Vega used the funds for her personal expenses.Vega pleaded guilty to four counts of wire fraud and one count of falsely impersonating a federal employee.The charges stem from her use of a fabricated government identity to persuade the victim to transfer money under false pretences. The case was announced by the US Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico, along with officials from the IRS Criminal Investigation division and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).At sentencing, Vega faces a maximum prison term of 20 years, a fine of up to $250,000 and an order to pay restitution to the victim. The amount of restitution will be determined by the court. However, Vega has not yet been sentenced, and the final punishment will be decided by the court.The investigation was conducted by the FBI's Albuquerque Field Office and IRS Criminal Investigation's Phoenix Field Office, with assistance from the Bernalillo County Sheriff's Office and the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration. The US Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico is prosecuting the case.The IRS has repeatedly warned taxpayers about scammers who impersonate its employees through phone calls, emails, text messages and social media. Such fraudsters may claim that a person is entitled to a refund, tax credit or government payment, or threaten legal consequences unless money is transferred immediately.According to the IRS, unexpected communications promising unusually large refunds or demanding immediate payments should be treated with caution. The agency advises taxpayers to independently verify suspicious communications rather than relying on phone numbers, links or contact details provided by the person approaching them. The IRS also says it generally initiates contact with taxpayers through letters or notices delivered by the US Postal Service. It does not send unsolicited social media direct messages or demand immediate payment through gift cards.In a separate warning about tax-related scams, the agency has highlighted how fraudsters exploit the possibility of receiving large refunds or credits to convince people to share personal and financial information or pay upfront fees. The US government's consumer protection guidance similarly warns that impersonation scams often involve individuals claiming to represent official agencies, businesses or other trusted organisations. Their objective is to gain a victim's confidence before requesting money or sensitive information.The IRS recommends checking whether a communication is genuine before responding to requests for money or personal information. Taxpayers who receive suspicious calls can hang up and contact the agency through its official website or verified telephone numbers. The agency also advises people not to click on suspicious links or share sensitive financial information in response to unexpected messages claiming to offer refunds or tax benefits.Vega's case involved a victim who continued making payments over several years in the expectation of receiving a large government payout. With her guilty plea, the case now moves towards sentencing, where the court will determine the prison term, financial penalty and restitution owed to the victim.
Article Summary: Sandra Vega, 48, of Pecos, New Mexico, has pleaded guilty to five federal charges in connection with the fraud scheme. She convinced a victim that he would receive a large sum of money from the US tax agency if he first paid various fees and deposits. The victim handed over at least $150,000, believing the money would be transferred to the IRS, but the woman allegedly spent it on personal expenses. Vega faces a maximum prison term of 20 years, a fine of up to $250,000 and an order to pay restitution to the victim.

Article Title: No strikes, no peace deal: How Trump plans to keep Iran under pressure
Article Text:
No strikes, no peace deal: How Trump plans to tighten the screws on Iran

US President Donald Trump has settled on a third option in the Iran war, choosing to intensify economic pressure on Tehran rather than resume military strikes or agree to a peace deal on terms Washington considers unacceptable, according to an Axios report.US secretary of state Marco Rubio outlined the administration's approach during a meeting with G7 foreign ministers on Tuesday, saying Trump was not limited to choosing between renewed military action and a negotiated agreement with Iran.Instead, Washington plans to continue its existing pressure campaign and further tighten the financial squeeze on Tehran, Axios reported."The President doesn't just have two options. It's not just returning to war or signing a ridiculous peace deal. We won't do a stupid deal. The third option we have is to continue to do what we do now," Rubio said.He argued that maintaining the current strategy would steadily increase the financial burden on Tehran without forcing Washington to set a deadline for ending the pressure campaign.The strategy aims to weaken Iran's financial infrastructure to the point where it struggles to fund armed groups or rebuild its military capabilities.Rubio also argued that Tehran was inflicting serious damage on its own economy by refusing to accept Washington's conditions."The President is not under false time pressure, the Iranians are inflicting major damage on their own economy," Rubio mentioned.The approach comes after months of uncertainty over the direction of the conflict. Trump has repeatedly threatened devastating military action against Iran while insisting that Tehran would eventually give in to Washington's demands. The conflict has also become a domestic political liability, with Republican candidates suffering setbacks in the midterm legislative contests.An American official close to the administration told Axios that Trump had been weighing several options without being certain which course to pursue. However, after meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on Monday, Trump signalled that he preferred to avoid another round of military strikes.He described the possibility of fresh attacks on Iranian targets as highly unlikely and unnecessary under the current circumstances.The administration instead plans to maintain its economic offensive and naval blockade while pursuing a new operation, 'Iron Gate'. The operation is aimed at dismantling ground transportation routes allegedly used to smuggle advanced weapons and technology.According to administration sources cited by Axios, Rubio was among the key figures in Trump's national security team who advocated this approach. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent, CIA director John Ratcliffe and presidential adviser Jared Kushner were also involved in the discussions.The officials reportedly opposed a renewed military escalation, arguing that Iran's current negotiating position remained fundamentally at odds with American interests. They favoured maintaining stringent financial pressure on the regime instead.Rubio also expressed doubts about the prospects of an immediate diplomatic breakthrough, saying Iran's preconditions for formal negotiations were unworkable. Speaking to reporters after the G7 ministerial meeting, he said Tehran wanted an agreement but had failed to put forward constructive proposals.He suggested that prolonged economic pressure would eventually force Iran to reconsider its position, as mounting financial difficulties would become increasingly difficult for its leadership to sustain."Eventually you have to eat," Rubio said, suggesting that basic material realities would eventually sway even the most uncompromising factions within the Iranian hierarchy.However, Washington's strategy of maintaining an extended economic squeeze has raised concerns among some of its key regional partners, including Turkey, Pakistan and Iraq, an administration official told Axios.The three countries reportedly have reservations about Washington's preference for indefinite financial pressure over efforts to secure a stable, negotiated settlement with Tehran.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has settled on a third option in the Iran war. He plans to intensify economic pressure on Tehran rather than resume military strikes or agree to a peace deal. US secretary of state Marco Rubio outlined the administration's approach during a meeting with G7 foreign ministers on Tuesday.

Article Title: A Navy veteran’s 1946 letter to his high-school sweetheart was sealed inside an Illinois home’s wall; renovators found it 70 years later and returned it to him at age 90
Article Text:
Representative AI image of a 90-year-old man revisiting a long-lost love letter. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

A wartime letter hidden inside a home

Renovators trace the letter’s original writer

Two U.S. Navy recruits write letters during their training in the 1940s, reflecting the wartime correspondence that connected servicemen with their loved ones back home. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A personal reminder of wartime relationship

The letter was written by a young US Navy sailor to his high school sweetheart in April 1946. It was found inside the wall of a home in Illinois several decades later. When the letter was discovered and returned to the 90-year-old sailor in October 2016, a tender reunion between a man and his long-lost love took place. Lt. McCabe, the man who penned the words in the letter, addressed it to a young woman named Juanita Gibbs.Tom Moore and his wife, Laura, found the letter during the renovation of an old house in Quincy, Illinois, where it had been buried in loose packing paper removed from a wall. They found the correspondence with the name on it, ‘ Lt. Kenneth L. McCabe,’ and the intended recipient, Juanita Gibbs. It was dated April 1946, placing it after the Second World War had ended. By the time he wrote it, the Navy vet was assisting in Guam, having spent about a year and a half in the service, including in the South Pacific.Apparently, neither of them received the letter, or they did but never opened it, so it was stored away in the building. What that letter gave us, in any case, was a peek at a relationship that had started well before he had even penned that letter.According to the Navy Times, McCabe described that she was the girl he dated in high school and fell in love with before he got down on one knee and married her on October 25, 1947. They had three kids, and they were together until she passed away.Instead of treating the old letter as a mundane object to be thrown away, he decided to try to track down the person the letter was addressed to. Moore started ringing around and searching for McCabe to see if he could determine whether he was alive and to try to get in touch with him. He sought advice from a friend, who told him to look into a local Honor Flight group. Honor Flight is a not-for-profit organisation that arranges trips to national memorials for eligible military personnel, with a particular focus on those who served in the Second World War and subsequent conflicts.The resolution to search brought a simple home renovation to a joyful conclusion. Moore was able to place the letter in McCabe's hands at his work. Marine Corps Times reported that the other workers gathered around the man as he accepted the historic letter and applauded him as he was able to reconnect to the lifetime period it documented. It was especially poignant to reestablish the relationship since Juanita wasn't around to get the letter.McCabe was amazed that the letter was still intact. “When I think back to Juanita, I just remember the good wife and mother she was,” he said, adding that he appreciated the effort Moore went into returning the correspondence instead of throwing it away. “I am really looking forward to getting back home and sitting down and reading what I wrote all those years ago, because it wasn't just the one letter I wrote.” The note from McCabe adds weight to the significance of personal letters, especially those retained during lengthy military separation.Sending a letter home was a vital part of communication between servicemen and those left behind. Personal notes can preserve everyday emotions and intimate concerns that official accounts do not tend to reveal. For McCabe, this letter wasn't just a piece from the past; it was a bridge back to his youth, to the Navy, and to the woman he considered his first love.
Article Summary: The letter was written by a young US Navy sailor to his high school sweetheart in April 1946. It was found inside the wall of a home in Illinois several decades later. Lt. Kenneth L. McCabe, the man who penned the words in the letter, addressed it to a young woman named Juanita Gibbs.

Article Title: Kenan Thompson and Luis Guzman are hosting a New York gala for a charity fighting childhood brain cancer; the Cristian Rivera Foundation says it has donated over $4 million to research and family supp
Article Text:
Inspired by a loss

$365,000 donation supports research at Weill Cornell

What is DIPG?

Actor and comedian Kenan Thompson and actor Luis Guzman were named among the hosts of the 17th Annual Cristian Rivera Foundation Celebrity Gala, a fundraising event scheduled for November 10 at Cipriani Wall Street in New York City. According to the foundation's official announcement, the organisation has donated more than $4 million towards research into diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG), a rare and aggressive childhood brain tumour, as well as financial assistance for affected families.The event, which also featured NBC's Darlene Rodriguez as a host, was organised to raise funds for clinical trials, medical research and family support programmes. The evening's programme was scheduled to include a red-carpet reception, dinner, an awards ceremony, live and silent auctions, and a video presentation highlighting the experiences of children and families affected by the disease.According to the foundation, proceeds from the gala will support research and clinical trials led by Dr Mark Souweidane at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and Weill Cornell Medical College, along with research conducted by Dr Oren Becher at Mount Sinai Kravis Children's Hospital.A portion of the funds will also go towards providing direct financial assistance to families dealing with DIPG.The organisation's origins are rooted in the personal tragedy of its founder, John "Gungie" Rivera, who established the Cristian Rivera Foundation in 2009 after losing his son to DIPG. According to the foundation's account, Cristian Alexander Rivera was diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumour on January 22, 2007. He was four years old at the time. Despite receiving treatment at Memorial Sloan Kettering and Weill Cornell Medical Center, the child died on January 25, 2009, after fighting the disease for two years.His father's experience prompted him to establish the New Jersey-based nonprofit with the aim of funding research towards a cure, spreading awareness and helping families navigate the challenges of a childhood cancer diagnosis. The foundation says it has since become one of the country's major private financial supporters of DIPG research. Its work also includes providing information, resources and monetary assistance to families affected by the disease.In January 2026, the organisation announced a $365,000 donation to Weill Cornell Medicine, its largest single contribution to date. According to a January 8 report by Weill Cornell Medicine, Thompson joined Rivera in presenting the donation to Dr Mark Souweidane, vice chair of the Department of Neurological Surgery and director of paediatric neurological surgery at NewYork-Presbyterian Komansky Children's Hospital.The contribution will support Souweidane's research into developing more effective, targeted treatments for children diagnosed with DIPG. The foundation said the donation was raised through its fundraising initiatives, including its annual celebrity gala.A February 2026 report by Inside Philanthropy also noted that the foundation had crossed the $4 million mark in cumulative donations towards DIPG research and family support.DIPG is a fast-growing tumour that develops in the pons, a part of the brainstem responsible for several vital functions, including breathing, heart rate and movement. According to the US National Cancer Institute, approximately 300 children are diagnosed with the condition in the country every year.The tumour is particularly difficult to treat because of its location and its tendency to spread into surrounding healthy brain tissue. Most children diagnosed with DIPG do not survive longer than two years, the institute says. There is currently no established cure for the disease, making research into new treatment approaches and clinical trials particularly important.
Article Summary: Kenan Thompson and Luis Guzman hosted the 17th Annual Cristian Rivera Foundation Celebrity Gala in New York City on November 10. The event was organised to raise funds for clinical trials, medical research and family support programmes. The organisation has donated more than $4 million towards research into diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG), a rare and aggressive childhood brain tumour.

Article Title: 'Got rid of her like garbage': Nepali-American man convicted of wife's murder in US
Article Text:
Mamta Kafle murder: US jury finds husband guilty of first-degree murder

Bhatt's past in the US
